**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Paper 2: Section A - Summary and Text Reconstruction; Section B - Composition; Section C - Prescribed Texts. Duration: three hours.**

Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will be penalised.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised composition will be severely sanctioned.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **c)** Describe an incident that occurred as a result of a rumour, showing the consequences and bringing out the lessons learned from it.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: the image of the spark in dry grass; the market in Bafoussam.
2. The rumour starts and grows from stall to stall.
3. The panic: the crowd at the bank, injuries, theft, police.
4. The truth emerges: a computer breakdown, exaggerated.
5. Lessons: check information, do not repeat it, trust reliable sources.

**Model composition (524 words)**

A rumour is like a spark in dry grass: it begins small, but once the wind catches it, nobody can control where it will go. I learnt this truth in March last year, when a single sentence turned an ordinary market day in Bafoussam into a scene of fear and loss.

It was a Saturday, and the central market was crowded with traders and buyers. I had gone there with my mother to buy foodstuff for the week. As we bargained over a heap of tomatoes, a woman rushed past, breathless, and whispered to the seller, "Have you heard? They say that the bank across the road has collapsed and that all the money of the traders is gone!" The seller's face turned pale. Within seconds the news passed from stall to stall, growing larger at each telling. By the time it reached the end of our row, the bank had been robbed, the manager had run away, and the army was on its way.

Nobody stopped to ask who had said it. The traders, who kept all their savings in that bank, abandoned their goods and ran towards the building. Others followed simply because everyone else was running. The street was soon packed with shouting people pushing, pulling and falling over each other. A motorbike taxi knocked down an old woman, a boy's leg was trampled, and in the confusion thieves moved among the stalls, carrying away bags of rice, cloth and phones.

At the bank, the doors were firmly closed because it was lunchtime, and the guards, frightened by the crowd, called the police. The security forces arrived with sirens and tear gas, and the panic became a riot. My mother held my hand so tightly that it hurt, and we were carried along the road like leaves in a flood until we found shelter in a shop. When the dust settled, three people were in hospital, many traders had lost their goods, and a young shopkeeper had lost the savings of a year to thieves.

Then the truth emerged. The manager came out calmly and explained that the bank was working normally; the only problem had been a short breakdown of its computers that morning, which a careless customer had misunderstood and exaggerated to a friend. Nobody had intended harm, yet the damage was serious and could not be undone. The woman who started the story was never found, and the traders who suffered could only blame themselves for believing her.

That Saturday taught me lessons I have never forgotten. First, information must be checked before it is believed, and certainly before it is passed on, because every person who repeats a rumour becomes a part of its harm. Second, fear is a poor adviser: those who ran fastest were the ones who lost most. Third, the community must trust reliable sources, such as official announcements and responsible journalists, rather than whispers in a crowd. Since that day, whenever a startling story reaches me, I pause and ask a simple question: "Who says so, and how do they know?" That small habit, I believe, could save many a market from chaos.

**Marking grid (20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Describing a rumour in general terms instead of one incident with a clear sequence of events.
2. Giving the consequences but omitting the lessons learned, which the topic demands.
